title: Sounds First — The Deep Dive

pts: Segmental features are individual vowels and consonants; suprasegmental features are stress, rhythm and intonation.
Research consistently finds suprasegmental errors damage intelligibility more than segmental ones.
A lesson plan weighted entirely toward individual sounds is solving the smaller problem.

items: Write I didn’t say she took the money. on the board.
Say it seven times, each time stressing a different word. After each version, ask learners what extra meaning it carries.
Learners work in pairs: one says the sentence with stress on a chosen word; the other chooses the matching meaning from a list.
Contrast with a segmental task: say ship and sheep. Ask which difference, the sentence stress or the vowel, made more change to meaning in these examples.
Discuss: which should we practise more?
Use a shorter sentence for lower levels: I like your bag.
Learners write their own sentence with three possible meanings.
Support: underline the stressed word on the board as you say each version.
Stretch: learners explain the meaning in a full sentence (…but someone else did.).

lines: I didn’t say she took the money. (Someone else said it.)
I didn’t say she took the money. (I only suggested it.)
I didn’t say she took the money. (Someone else took it.)
I didn’t say she took the money. (She took something else.)
Segmental: individual vowels and consonants (/iː/ vs /ɪ/, /v/ vs /w/).
Suprasegmental: word stress, sentence stress, rhythm, intonation.

body: Purpose: to show where teaching time is usually spent and where it may be needed. Content: an iceberg in water. Above the waterline, a small tip labelled ‘individual sounds’. Below the waterline, a much larger mass labelled with ‘word stress’, ‘sentence stress’, ‘rhythm’, ‘intonation’, ‘linking’. A small boat labelled ‘typical lesson’ circles the tip. Style: simple, cool colours, labels clearly legible. Board version: a triangle split by a line.

items: YouGlish (free). Search a short phrase to hear how stress falls in real speech by many speakers; choose clips in advance.

blocks.x: Your voice and the class’s voices. Exaggerate stress at first, then return to natural speech.

pts: Most English use today is between non-native speakers — native-like accent is not the useful target.
The Lingua Franca Core identifies the specific features (like consonant clusters) that cause real misunderstanding between L2 speakers.
Features outside the core — like the 'th' sounds — can often be safely deprioritised.
points.who: Jennifer Jenkins, "The Phonology of English as an International Language"

items: Explain that some features matter more than others for being understood internationally. Consonant clusters are one.
Say words with initial and final clusters: street, school, strength, asked, texts, months. Learners repeat.
Point out that adding a vowel (/ɪskuːl/ for school, /stɪriːt/ for street) usually keeps the word understandable, while dropping a consonant (as for asked) can change the word.
In pairs, learners read sentences containing clusters; the partner writes the word heard.
Collect words that partners misheard. Practise only those.
Make a ‘cluster ladder’: eat – seat – sweet – street.
Use learners’ own town and street names.
Support: start with two-consonant clusters only.
Stretch: include clusters across word boundaries (next stop, last train).

blocks.x: Priorities from the Lingua Franca Core (simplified from Jenkins 2000):

lines: Keep: most consonant sounds; consonant clusters at the beginning of words; the difference between long and short vowels; nuclear (main) stress in a phrase.
Less critical: the th sounds /θ/ and /ð/; the ‘dark l’; weak forms; exact vowel quality.

blocks.x: Many Indian speakers pronounce th in think as a dental /t̪/. This is a consistent feature of Indian English and rarely causes misunderstanding; class time is usually better spent elsewhere.

body: Purpose: to show teaching priorities. Content: two concentric circles. The inner circle, shaded, labelled ‘Core: teach and practise’, with examples (consonants, clusters, long/short vowels, main stress). The outer ring, lightly shaded, labelled ‘Useful for listening; lower priority for speaking’, with examples (th, dark l, weak forms, exact vowel quality). Style: calm, two shades of one colour. Board version: two circles and lists.

items: Cambridge Dictionary online (free). Play both UK and US recordings of the same word to show that different accents are all intelligible models.

blocks.x: Mouth diagrams drawn on the board, and a hand mirror passed round so learners can see their own lips and tongue.

body: Jenkins’s Lingua Franca Core was based on observing breakdowns in conversations between non-native speakers of English. It was designed as a guide for teachers of English as an international language, not as a description of any single accent, and it remains debated. Use it as a starting point for your own diagnosis rather than as a fixed syllabus.

pts: Minimal pairs (ship/sheep) are useful for confusions that genuinely cause misunderstanding for a given L1 group.
Overused, they drill sounds in isolation that rarely appear that way in connected speech.
Diagnose the learner's actual confusions before choosing which pairs are worth class time.

v: Two cards per learner, labelled 1 and 2; a list of word pairs chosen from your diagnosis

items: Before the lesson, listen to learners speaking and reading aloud. Note the two or three sound confusions that actually cause misunderstanding.
Write a pair on the board: 1 wet, 2 vet. Say one word; learners hold up the matching card.
Repeat with several pairs, mixing the order.
Put the words in sentences: Take the dog to the (wet/vet). Learners choose.
Learners take turns saying a word to a partner, who holds up a card. Swap.
Stop after 10–15 minutes and move on. Return to the same pairs briefly in later lessons.
Use pictures instead of words for young learners.
Make a ‘stepping stones’ game: learners walk on stone 1 or 2 according to the word heard.
Support: start with pairs that differ in more than one feature (fan / bun).
Stretch: add a third option (wet / vet / bet).

blocks.x: Choosing pairs by diagnosis, not by list. Examples of pairs that might be worth practising for some Indian learners, depending on what you hear:

lines: /v/–/w/: vet – wet, vest – west (many speakers use one sound for both)
/iː/–/ɪ/: sheep – ship, leave – live
/s/–/ʃ/: sip – ship, sea – she
/z/–/dʒ/: zest – jest (in some regions)

body: Purpose: a photocopiable card set. Content: pairs of picture cards: a wet umbrella and a veterinary surgeon with a dog; a ship and a sheep; a seat and a sheet; a fan and a van. Each card has the word in large letters below the picture and a small number 1 or 2 in the corner. Style: bold outline drawings, easy to cut out. Board version: two columns of words.

items: Sounds Right (free phonemic chart app from the British Council). Tap a symbol to hear the sound and example words. [VERIFY current availability on Android and iOS.]

blocks.x: Your voice and the number cards. Stand at the back of the room sometimes, so learners do not rely on watching your lips.

pts: English is stress-timed: stressed syllables fall at roughly even intervals, unlike syllable-timed languages.
Shifting stress changes word class — 'REcord' the noun versus 'reCORD' the verb.
Mis-stressed words are often simply unrecognised by a listener, even if every phoneme is correct.

v: Two cards per learner: N and V

items: Write record on the board. Say REcord and reCORD. Ask which is the noun and which the verb.
Say the words below in random order, with noun or verb stress. Learners hold up N or V.
Give sentences with the word missing: Can I ___ your voice? / This is a ___ of the meeting. Learners say the sentence with the right stress.
Learners test each other in pairs.
Discuss the pattern: many two-syllable noun–verb pairs have stress on the first syllable for the noun and the second for the verb.
Extend to word families where stress moves: PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy, photoGRAphic.
Make a class list of words that follow and do not follow the pattern.
Support: work with three pairs only.
Stretch: find exceptions (reply, control keep second-syllable stress as nouns).

lines: REcord / reCORD; PREsent / preSENT; OBject / obJECT; CONtract / conTRACT; PROduce / proDUCE; INcrease / inCREASE

blocks.x: Why stress errors matter: a listener searching for deVElopment may not recognize DEvelopment at all, even if every sound is clear.

body: Purpose: to show the noun–verb pattern. Content: a two-column table headed ‘Noun’ and ‘Verb’. Each row shows the same word twice with the stressed syllable in bold capitals and a large dot above it: REcord / reCORD, PREsent / preSENT, OBject / obJECT. A small arrow between the columns shows the dot moving right. Style: clean table, one accent colour for the dots. Board version: two columns, dots drawn above syllables.

items: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries online (free). Entries show stress marks in the phonemic transcription; learners can check noun and verb forms separately.

blocks.x: Mark stress in vocabulary notebooks with a small circle above the stressed syllable. Make this a routine for every new word of two or more syllables.

pts: Linking, elision and assimilation reshape words in the stream of speech — 'want to' becomes 'wanna'.
Teach connected speech for listening comprehension first; learners need to recognise it before producing it.
Untaught, connected speech is one of the biggest gaps between classroom English and real audio.

v: Sentences with typical linking and weak forms

items: Say a sentence naturally: Fish and chips. Ask learners to write what they heard.
Show the written form. Explain that and often becomes /ən/ or /n/.
Continue with more sentences, each showing one feature: linking, weak forms, elision, assimilation (see model language).
After each sentence, learners compare what they wrote with a partner, then check.
Learners practise saying the sentences slowly, then naturally. Emphasize that recognizing these forms comes first; producing them is optional.
Use song lyrics (short extracts you are permitted to use) to find linked words.
Learners mark links with a curved line in a printed dialogue.
Support: provide the sentences with gaps where the reduced words are.
Stretch: learners find examples in a short video clip.

lines: Linking: an apple → /ə ˈnæpl/
Weak form: a cup of tea → /ə ˈkʌp ə ˈtiː/
Elision (a sound disappears): next day → /neks deɪ/
Assimilation (a sound changes): ten boys → /tem bɔɪz/
Common reductions in informal speech: going to → gonna, want to → wanna

body: Purpose: to make invisible links visible. Content: three short sentences in large type (an apple, turn it off, a cup of tea) with curved arcs drawn beneath joining the end of one word to the start of the next. Weak syllables shown in smaller, lighter type. Style: clear typography; arcs in the accent colour. Board version: sentences with chalk arcs.

items: ELLLO (free). Short recordings with transcripts; learners find and underline linked words in the transcript while listening.

blocks.x: Read a short dialogue aloud twice: once word by word and once naturally. Learners mark where the words ‘joined’.

pts: Rising and falling tunes signal question type, certainty, and whether a speaker has finished their turn.
The same words with different intonation can sound genuinely interested or flatly bored.
Drill intonation through short authentic dialogue, not isolated sentences read off a page.

v: Cards with feelings (interested, bored, surprised, angry, polite)

items: Say Oh, really? with a wide, rising tune, then with a flat, low tune. Ask learners how you feel each time.
Give each learner a feeling card secretly.
Learners say a short phrase (That’s nice. / Really? / Thank you.) in the manner of their card. The class guesses the feeling.
Present a short dialogue. Learners mark rising (↗) or falling (↘) tunes before practising it in pairs.
Discuss when a flat tune might sound rude in English even if the words are polite.
Hum the tune of a sentence without words (the ‘kazoo’ technique); learners guess the sentence.
Record two versions of the same dialogue with different tunes and discuss the difference.
Support: work with two feelings only (interested and bored).
Stretch: learners explain how tune changes a question from checking to real asking (You’re coming?).

lines: It’s raining. ↘ (a statement)
It’s raining? ↗ (surprise or checking)
Thank you. ↘ with a wide fall (warm) / flat and low (cold or dismissive)
A: I’ve got a new job. ↘
B: Really? ↗ That’s great! ↘

body: Purpose: to show intonation visually. Content: three short phrases each with a curved line above the words: a wide falling curve over Thank you (labelled ‘warm’), a flat low line over the same words (labelled ‘cold’), a rising curve over Really? (labelled ‘surprised’). Style: simple lines, one colour per feeling. Board version: chalk curves above words.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in). Learners record themselves saying a phrase in two ways and play it to a partner.

blocks.x: Hand movements: learners draw the tune in the air with a finger as they speak.

body: When learners sound impolite in English, the cause is often intonation rather than vocabulary. Before teaching another polite phrase, try teaching the tune that goes with the phrases they already know.

pts: Underhill's phonemic chart groups sounds by mouth position, giving learners a map instead of a list.
Learners can locate and self-correct a sound using the chart, independent of the teacher's own accent.
Introduce the chart gradually — a handful of high-value symbols at a time, not all 44 at once.

v: 10 minutes a lesson over several weeks
A phonemic chart (large poster or board version); a pointer

items: Introduce the chart as a map of sounds, not a test. Show how it is organized: vowels at the top, consonants below; sounds near each other are made in similar places in the mouth.
Each week, teach six symbols. Choose ones that are useful for your learners (for example /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʃ/, /v/, /w/, /ə/).
Point to a symbol; learners say the sound. Say a sound; a learner points.
When a learner mispronounces a word, point to the target symbol instead of saying the word again. The learner self-corrects.
Learners start writing the key symbol beside new words in their notebooks.
Make a ‘chart walk’ on the floor with symbols on paper squares; learners step on the sounds of a word.
Play ‘symbol bingo’.
Support: pair each symbol with a picture word (a ship for /ɪ/).
Stretch: learners transcribe a short word using the symbols they know.

lines: S1: I leeve in Hubballi.
T: [points to /ɪ/]
S1: I live in Hubballi.

blocks.x: A teaching order for the first six weeks (adapt to your learners): /ɪ/ /iː/ /ə/ – /ʃ/ /s/ /z/ – /v/ /w/ /f/ – /æ/ /e/ /ʌ/ – /θ/ /ð/ (recognition only) – /aɪ/ /eɪ/ /əʊ/.

body: Purpose: a classroom reference. Content: a grid of phonemic symbols for British English arranged in the style of Underhill’s chart: monophthongs top left, diphthongs top right, consonants below in voiceless/voiced pairs. Each symbol has a tiny example word beneath it. Symbols taught so far are shown in bold; the rest are pale. Style: large, legible symbols (minimum 24 pt when printed A3). Board version: draw only the symbols taught so far. Note to designer: create an original layout; do not reproduce a published chart.

items: Sounds Right (British Council, free). An interactive chart that plays each sound and example words.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn chart on chart paper, added to week by week, so it grows with the class.

pts: The realistic, research-backed goal is intelligibility — being understood — not the elimination of an accent.
Treating an L1-influenced accent as a problem to fix can be both inaccurate and demotivating.
Correct only the features that measurably interfere with being understood.
points.who: Jennifer Jenkins on intelligibility over nativeness

v: Ten sentences on slips; answer sheets

items: Give each pair ten sentence slips.
S1 reads a sentence aloud without showing it. S2 writes down what they heard.
Pairs compare the written sentence with the slip. They circle only the words that were misunderstood.
Swap roles.
As a class, collect the circled words. Discuss the cause of each (a sound, a stress, speed). Practise only those.
Emphasize: the aim was to be understood, and most sentences were.
Pair learners who share a home language, then pairs who do not, and compare the results.
Use real messages: directions, a phone message, a short announcement.
Support: shorter sentences with familiar words.
Stretch: learners read a short paragraph and the listener summarizes it.

lines: S2: I heard west. Did you say vest?
S1: Yes, vest, like a shirt.
Accent: how different a speaker sounds from a listener’s expectations.
Comprehensibility: how easy the speaker is to understand.
Intelligibility: how much of the message is actually understood.

blocks.x: A speaker can have a strong accent and be completely intelligible.

body: Purpose: to show that the three are related but different. Content: three overlapping circles in a Venn arrangement labelled ‘Accent’, ‘Comprehensibility’, ‘Intelligibility’. In the area outside ‘Accent’ but inside the other two, a small figure with a speech bubble labelled ‘strong accent, fully understood’. Style: soft colours, clear labels. Board version: three circles.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in). Learners record the ten sentences at the start of term and again at the end; a partner who does not share their home language checks intelligibility each time.

blocks.x: The partner-dictation task in the activity needs only paper.

body: Record one of your learners reading a short paragraph. Play it to a colleague from a different language background and ask them to write down what they understood. Circle what was lost. The result is usually a much shorter list than you would guess, and a much more useful one.

dek: Unit 4 of 100: pronunciation teaching that prioritises intelligibility over accent — from the sounds that actually cause miscommunication to the intonation that carries meaning.

aims.x: This unit takes the brief look at pronunciation in Unit 1 and goes deeper. Its guiding principle is that the goal of pronunciation teaching is to be understood, not to sound like any particular native speaker, and that the features which most affect being understood are often not the ones teachers spend most time on.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish segmental from suprasegmental features and explain why the second matter so much;
use the Lingua Franca Core to decide which sounds deserve class time;
diagnose which sound contrasts cause real confusion for your learners;
teach word stress, connected speech and intonation as meaningful features;
introduce the phonemic chart gradually as a tool for independence;
respond to accent with respect while working on intelligibility.

why: Why this matters. Unit 1 flagged phonology as foundational. Most pronunciation teaching over-invests in individual sounds and under-invests in the stress and rhythm that most affect intelligibility.

background.x: Pronunciation is the part of language that people hear first and judge fastest. It is also, in many classrooms, the part that is taught least systematically. Teachers often feel unsure of their own models, or remember pronunciation lessons from their own schooling as repetitive drilling of sounds with little obvious purpose.

Two changes in thinking over the last thirty years make the task clearer. The first is a shift of attention from individual sounds (segmentals) to the rhythm, stress and melody of speech (suprasegmentals). Studies of intelligibility suggest that listeners are often more thrown by misplaced stress or unfamiliar rhythm than by an unusual vowel (Derwing and Munro 2015). The second is the recognition that most spoken English today is used between people for whom it is not a first language. Jennifer Jenkins (2000) studied such interactions and identified the features that most often caused breakdowns; she called this set the Lingua Franca Core. Her work gives teachers a principled way to choose what to teach.

For Indian learners, this matters a great deal. Indian English is a well-established variety with its own consistent patterns of sound and rhythm (Sailaja 2009). It is not a set of errors. The practical question for a teacher is therefore not ‘How do I remove my learners’ accent?’ but ‘Which features, if any, get in the way of being understood by the people my learners will talk to?’ This unit gives you ways to answer that question and to act on the answer.

items: Intelligibility check. Repeat the ‘Understood?’ task each term with new sentences. Track the percentage of words correctly understood by a partner.
Stress recognition quiz. Say ten words; learners mark the stressed syllable. Include noun–verb pairs.
Chart use. Note how often learners self-correct when you point to a symbol. Increasing self-correction is a sign of growing independence.
Recorded reading. Learners record a short text at the start and end of a unit; compare for stress and intonation.
How confident do you feel about your own pronunciation as a model? What would make you more confident?
Which pronunciation features do you usually correct? Are they the ones that cause misunderstanding?
What does your class believe about ‘good’ English pronunciation? Where do those beliefs come from?
How much class time goes on individual sounds, and how much on stress and intonation?
How would you respond to a learner who says, ‘I want to sound like a British person’?

reading: Derwing, T. M. and M. J. Munro. 2015. Pronunciation Fundamentals: Evidence-based Perspectives for L2 Teaching and Research. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Gilbert, J. B. 2008. Teaching Pronunciation: Using the Prosody Pyramid. New York: Cambridge University Press.
Jenkins, J. 2000. The Phonology of English as an International Language. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Levis, J. M. 2018. Intelligibility, Oral Communication, and the Teaching of Pronunciation. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Roach, P. 2009. English Phonetics and Phonology: A Practical Course. 4th edn. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Sailaja, P. 2009. Indian English. Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press.
Underhill, A. 2005. Sound Foundations: Learning and Teaching Pronunciation. 2nd edn. Oxford: Macmillan.

terms.def: The features of pronunciation that identify where a speaker comes from or which group they belong to; every speaker has an accent, and an Indian accent is no barrier to being understood.
In connected speech, the change of a sound so that it becomes more like a neighbouring sound, as when ten boys is pronounced with an m sound at the end of ten.
How easily a listener can understand a speaker, as judged by the listener’s effort; a speaker with a strong accent can still be highly comprehensible.
Natural, fluent speech in which sounds in neighbouring words change, link or disappear, as when want to becomes wanna; learners need practice in hearing it.
A group of two or more consonant sounds together without a vowel between them, as in street or texts; some learners add a vowel to break clusters.
The loss of a sound in connected speech, as when next day is pronounced /neks deɪ/ or mustn’t loses its /t/. Recognizing elision helps learners understand natural, fast speech.
The extent to which a speaker’s words can be understood by listeners. Many teachers now aim for international intelligibility rather than a native-speaker accent (Jenkins 2000).
The rise and fall of pitch in speech, which signals meaning, attitude and information structure, such as the difference between a question and a statement.

A set of pronunciation features, identified by Jennifer Jenkins (2000), that appear most important for intelligibility when English is used between non-native speakers, such as most consonant sounds and nuclear stress.
In connected speech, the joining of the end of one word to the start of the next, as in an‿apple or go‿on, so that the words sound continuous.
A pair of words that differ in only one sound, such as ship and sheep or vest and west, used to help learners hear and produce sound contrasts that their first language may not make.
The smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning in a language, such as /p/ and /b/ in pin and bin.
A chart showing the phonemic symbols for the sounds of English, usually arranged by place and manner of articulation, used to teach and refer to pronunciation.

The individual sounds of a language, its consonants and vowels, as distinct from suprasegmental features such as stress and intonation. Examples include the difference between /v/ and /w/ or /ɪ/ and /iː/.

The pattern of strong and weak syllables across an utterance, in which content words carrying key meaning are stressed and many function words are reduced. It gives English its rhythm and highlights important information.

Features of pronunciation that extend over more than one sound, such as word stress, sentence stress, rhythm, intonation and connected speech. They often matter more for intelligibility than individual sounds.
The reduced pronunciation of a function word when unstressed, often with the vowel /ə/, such as /tə/ for to in ‘I want to go’. Weak forms are essential for natural rhythm and listening.
The emphasis given to one syllable in a word, such as PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy and photoGRAPHic. Misplaced stress can affect intelligibility more than individual sounds.
